CTMax Report Semifinal Draft

Introduction

  • Challenge of adaptation to climate change
  • Parallelism/ predictability in evolution
  • Atlantic salmon thermal tolerance
    • Importance of the freshwater environment
    • Previous studies on CTMax
  • Southern Newfoundland system
    • dual invasion (Brown Trout + Aquaculture salmon)

LR <- function(t, n) {
  return((1 + t**2)/(n-2))**(n/2)
}

Results

  • We found that salmon from a wild (historically introgressed) river (Tailrace Brook) had a higher critical thermal maximum than Brown Trout from a nearby river (Terrenceville Brook) or an aquaculture strain (Aquabounty) rasied at the Ocean Sciences Centre.
Code 
ggplot(meta %>% filter(FID != "TEBHybrid"), aes(x = FID, y = Temp_C)) + 
  geom_boxplot(colour = "darkblue") + 
  theme_bw() +
  ylab("Critical Thermal Maximum (C)")

Genomic underpinnings of thermal tolerance

Framing: we searched for parallelism in upper thermal tolerance by testing somewhat distantly related populations within the same genus.

PLINK Linear GWAS

For a PLINK GWAS, I used no covariates and ran each group separately. However, I could add weight as a covariate (this does not change the result much). I could also run the salmon groups together, though then the significant SNPs are mostly high FST SNPs between wild and aquaculture because of the difference in CTMax.

Brown Trout

system(paste(troutPath, "--bfile plinkFiles/troutCtMax --glm allow-no-covars --pheno plinkFiles/troutCtMaxPheno.tsv --pheno-name Temp_C --out plinkFiles/tebCTMaxGWAS"))

Expoloratory (likely will not include in the paper)

Looks like there is something going on with aquaculture effect size– maybe some SNPs that negatively impact CTMax? Here are the SNPs that have an effect size less than -1.5:

Code

              filter(BETA < -1.5) %>%  
              mutate(POSStart = POS - 1) %>% 
              mutate(POSend = POS + 1) %>% 
              select(c(`#CHROM`, POSStart, POSend, ID)),
  "plinkFiles/AqcNegativeBeta.bed", col.names = F, row.names = F, sep = "\t", quote = F)

Overlap in outlier SNPs and genes between wild, aquaculture, and trout

At the SNP level

I somewhat arbitrarily choose the 10,000 SNPs with the top LR. I used the same amount from each instead of a percentage because the dataset sizes differ somewhat substantially.

Gradient Boosting

Using subset of SNPs (top 1k LR) only to detect epistatic interactions and determine most important SNPs of this subset. Because we are starting with SNPs that are already known to be at least somewhat predictive in both groups, it is not to detect significance.

Potential to do: run a loop to test all SNPs with gradient boosting? Definite to-do: Run on DFO computer with 10K SNPs.

Code 
trbMeta <- meta %>% 
  filter(FID == "TRBSalmon") %>% 
  filter(!is.na(Temp_C)) %>% 
  distinct()

## Train/ test split is 70/30
indTRB <- sample(c(TRUE, FALSE), length(unique(trbMeta$IID)), replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.7, 0.3))

trainTRB <- trbMeta[indTRB, ]
testTRB <- trbMeta[!indTRB, ]

write.table(trainTRB %>% select(FID, IID) %>% distinct(), 
            file = "plinkFiles/TRBTrainCTmax.tsv", 
            col.names = F, 
            row.names = F, 
            sep = "\t", 
            quote = F)

write.table(testTRB %>% select(FID, IID) %>% distinct(), 
            file ="plinkFiles/TRBTestCTmax.tsv", 
            col.names = F, 
            row.names = F, 
            sep = "\t", 
            quote = F)

#rm(ad, ad2, ad3, aqcNegBeta, bim, chr, commonall, commonSNPs0, commonSNPs1, df_explainTEB, df_explainTRB, fam, eigenval, eigenvalSalmonLarge, eigenvalSalmon, fixed_snps, lm, long, missnps, NAInds, run1, run2, trainDataAQC, trainImpAQC, trainImpNAAQC, trainImpNATEB, trainImpTEB, troutGWAS10e4, x_predTRB, X_predTEB)


 TRBfam <- fread("plinkFiles/TRBTrainPLINKsnps.fam") %>% 
    rename("FID" = "V1",
           "IID" = "V2") %>%  #may need to fix this w/ PLINK2
    inner_join(meta) %>% 
    distinct()
  
  trainDataTRB <- fread("plinkFiles/TRBTrainPLINKsnps.raw", sep = "\t")  %>%  
    select (-FID, -IID, -PAT, -MAT, -SEX, -PHENOTYPE)
  
  trainImpTRB <- data.frame(apply(trainDataTRB, 2, function(x) replace(x, is.na(x), as.numeric(names(which.max(table(x))))))) 
  
  trainImpNATRB <- na.omit(cbind(trainImpTRB, TRBfam$Temp_C)) %>% 
  rename("CtMax" = "TRBfam$Temp_C")

TRBRecipe <- recipe(CtMax ~ ., data = trainImpNATRB) 
 ## need to giure out params!!


TRBxgboostModel <- boost_tree(trees = 200, tree_depth = 3, learn_rate = 0.2) %>%
  set_mode("regression") %>% 
  set_engine("xgboost")

TRBXgboostWf <- workflow(TRBRecipe, TRBxgboostModel)

TRBXgFit <- fit(TRBXgboostWf, trainImpNATRB)

#saveRDS(TRBXgFit, "plinkFiles/TRBXgFit1K.rds")
 
TRBXgImp <- xgb.importance(TRBXgFit$fit$fit$fit) %>% 
  mutate(Feature = sub('X', '', Feature)) %>% 
  mutate(ID = substr(Feature,1,nchar(Feature)-2)) %>% 
   arrange(desc(Gain)) %>% 
   separate_wider_delim(ID, delim = "_", names = c("Number", "POS")) %>% 
#  mutate(rank = row_number()) %>% 
  mutate(Group = "TRB")

SHAP Epistasis

SHAP, or SHapley Additive exPlanations, was developed by Lundberg and Lee (2017). This method provides each feature in a machine learning model with an importance value as well as interaction values. I am plotting these interaction values:

Code 
# SHAP analysis

df_explainTEB <- trainImpNATEB[1:69, ]

X_predTEB <- bake(  # Goes to xgboost:::predict.xgb.Booster()
  prep(tebRecipe), 
  has_role("predictor"),
  new_data = df_explainTEB,
  composition = "matrix"
)

stopifnot(colnames(X_predTEB) %in% colnames(df_explainTEB))

shap_valuesTEB <- extract_fit_engine(tebXgFit) |> 
  shapviz(X_pred = X_predTEB, X = df_explainTEB, interactions = TRUE)

#saveRDS(shap_valuesTEB, "shap_valuesTEB1K.rds")

# SHAP importance
# shap_values |> 
#   sv_importance(show_numbers = TRUE) +
#   ggtitle("SHAP importance")

# Absolute average SHAP interactions (off-diagonals already multiplied by 2)
shapdfTEB <- shap_valuesTEB |> 
  sv_interaction(kind = "no")


epTEB <- data.frame(shapdfTEB) %>% 
 filter(if_any(starts_with('X'), ~ . > 0.0001)) %>% 
  rownames_to_column() %>% 
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with('X')) %>% 
  filter(value > 0.0001) %>% 
  rename("SNP1" = "rowname",
         "SNP2" = "name",
          "shapInteractionValue" = "value") %>% 
  filter(SNP1 != SNP2) %>% 
  mutate(SNP1 = sub('X', '', SNP1)) %>% 
  mutate(SNP2 = sub('X', '', SNP2)) %>% 
  separate_wider_delim(SNP1, delim = "_", names = c("NC_SNP1", "POS_SNP1", "Nuc_SNP1")) %>% 
 # separate_wider_delim(POS_SNP1, delim = "_", names = c("POS_SNP1", "N1")) %>%
  #mutate(NC_SNP1 = paste0(NC_SNP1, ".1")) %>% 
  separate_wider_delim(SNP2, delim = "_", names = c("NC_SNP2", "POS_SNP2", "Nuc_SNP2")) %>% 
 # mutate(Group = "Trout") %>% 
  mutate(ID = paste(NC_SNP1, POS_SNP1, sep = "_")) %>% 
  merge(tebXgImp %>% 
          mutate(ID = paste(Number, POS, sep = "_")), by = "ID", all.x = TRUE) %>% 
  mutate(NC_SNP1 = as.numeric(NC_SNP1)) %>% 
  mutate(NC_SNP2 = as.numeric(NC_SNP2)) %>% 
  mutate(POS_SNP1 = as.numeric(POS_SNP1)) %>% 
  mutate(POS_SNP2 = as.numeric(POS_SNP2)) %>% 
  arrange(NC_SNP1, POS_SNP1)

One more analysis:

Are any of the outlier genes paralogs? There could be more parallelism between groups if this was the case. I am still figuring out how to conduct this analysis.

Discussion

Some potential points:

  • Perhaps a relaxation of selection in the aquaculture environment for thermal tolerance, since we would expect a higher thermal maximum due to being from a warmer environment originally
  • Potential for disruption to genomic architecture of wild fish from introgression from aquaculture. This is especially concerning for wild populations if the adaptation to thermal tolerance is non-parrallel with Newfoundland salmon.
  • Brown trout, a potential invasive species, had lower thermal tolerance than wild salmon, and had different genomic architecture. Because this particular population is the furthest west known population in Newfoundland (is this true?) we expect that genomic diversity may be lower than the rest of the population. Could mention hybidisation between salmon and trout, though not sure how relevant it is here. I did have three hybrid salmon/ trout samples and their thermal tolerance was intermediate.

Supplement

Salmon PCA (just dataset)

A PCA of all loci between aquaculture salmon and Tailrace Brook reveals significant genetic differences between these groups:

Code 
system(paste(troutPath, "--bfile plinkFiles/salmonCtMax --pca --maf --mind 0.2 --geno 0.2 --out plinkFiles/salmonCtmaxPCA"))
Code 
eigenvalSalmon <- fread("plinkFiles/salmonCtmaxPCA.eigenval")

fread("plinkFiles/salmonCtmaxPCA.eigenvec") %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, colour = `#FID`)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  theme_bw() + 
  labs(x = paste0("PC1 (", round(eigenvalSalmon$V1[1], digits = 2), "%)"), y = paste0("PC2 (", round(eigenvalSalmon$V1[2], digits = 2), "%)"))

Comparison to other populations

The question of how similar Aquabounty fish are to other aquaculture strains has been raised, as well as the extent of introgression in Tailrace Brook. To better understand this, we compared these samples to other populations in Newfoundland. Both Aquabounty and another aquaculture strian (USDA originating from the St. John River) had higher values on PC1, suggesting the sources of genetic variation due to aquaculture ancestry (either domestication selection or Saint John River founder effects) are similar between these samples. Tailrace Brook had more variation on PC2 than other NL rivers, but overlapped with nearby rivers that have experienced historical introgression (e.g. Conne). An admixture analysis shows fairly uniform estimates of aquaculture ancestry across individuals. There is no significant relationship between estimated aquaculture ancestry (using either admixture or PC1) and CTMax for Tailrace Fish.

Will likely not include these plots in the main MS, but perhaps in the supplement
